title: The Goddess Cuts the Serpent-Noose
story:
In the dark of Bana's prison, the young man who had routed an army had nothing left but his voice.

He had come to Sonitpura in the night, stolen from Dwaraka by illusion to marry a princess he had only ever seen in a dream — and the dream had kept its promise for a little while. Usha had chosen him by the boon of a goddess, her friend Chitralekha had carried him across the sky in secret, and for a few days the two had lived together as husband and wife in the women's quarters of the city. But when Bana, Bali's son, learned that his daughter was living with the Yadava prince, he had answered the leonine shout in the only way left to him: he seized Aniruddha and threw him into chains, there in his own city, together with Usha, who would not be parted from him. The hero of the field was now a prisoner, held by a strong noose of serpents, his strength useless and his club far away.

And it was there, in that darkness, that Aniruddha did the one thing left to him: he sought refuge with the goddess Kaumari, the maiden goddess, and sang her a hymn.

It was a careful song, and a knowing one. Saluting the endless, undecaying, eternal prime deity, the Lord Narayana, he chanted the glories of Chandi — the worshipful goddess Katyayani, whom all the gods and all the worlds worship, whom the gods, the rishis and the rakshasas alike adore, singing the very names that Hari sings. For his own well-being he bowed to her, the sister of Indra and of Vishnu, she who bestows honour and answers the prayers of her devotees. Cleansed and with a purified mind, his hands folded, he asked one thing only: “Release me from my bonds, and give me life and health.”

The goddess, fond of her votaries, heard him. Durga herself came to the place where Aniruddha lay in chains. She appeared before the young hero in the gloom of the cell, and consoled him; he saluted her, and then — with her own fingers, as easily as a mother loosens a knot — she cut the strong noose of serpents that held him.

And then she spoke. “O Aniruddha, wait here for a few days more. The holder of the discus, the slayer of the Daityas, will cut off the thousand arms of Vana, release you from your fetters, and take you to his own city.”

She did not carry him out of the prison. She cut his bonds, gave him a promise, and left him with something stronger than freedom: the certainty of rescue. Aniruddha waited — and across the sky, already flying toward Sonitpura on Garuda's back, came Krishna, Balarama and Pradyumna to make the goddess's words good.
reflection: The hymn is a prisoner's prayer that calls the goddess by her family — sister of Indra and of Vishnu — as though asking kin to remember one of their own. And Durga's answer is exact: she frees Aniruddha from despair, not from the prison, because Krishna's arrival is what will set him truly free.
next_story_tease: The goddess's promise pointed one way: across the sky, Krishna, Balarama and Pradyumna were already flying to Sonitpura on Garuda.
hero_scene: In the shadowy prison of Sonitpura, the great goddess Durga bends over the chained Aniruddha and, with her own fingers, cuts the strong noose of serpents that binds him, light breaking around her in the dark cell.
